name: Sweet clover (Melilotus)
short: Contains coumarins. Case report: severe liver dysfunction in a woman on interferon beta-1b who took a melilot supplement. The anticoagulant dicoumarol was found in spoiled sweet clover.
text: Sweet clover species (Melilotus albus and Melilotus officinalis) are used in herbal medicine because of their coumarins, and a laboratory study of 93 plant samples found that coumarin content varied significantly between them. A pharmacology review states that the anticoagulant medicine dicoumarol, a vitamin K antagonist, was discovered from the spoilage of Melilotus officinalis, and a review of herbal remedies and anticoagulant therapy notes that warfarin was originally derived from the sweet clover plant and that many herbs can increase the risk of bleeding when combined with warfarin, and another review lists sweet clover among herbal products that may potentially increase the risk of bleeding or the effects of warfarin, noting that nearly all such information comes from laboratory data, animal studies or individual case reports; the cited abstracts do not report bleeding in people taking sweet clover products, with or without anticoagulants. A case report described a 23-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis who had taken a melilot supplement containing coumarin for 3 years and developed severe liver dysfunction 14 days after starting interferon beta-1b injections; her liver tests returned to normal after both were stopped, and the authors suggest the supplement should be avoided by patients receiving interferon therapy. The interactions named in the cited sources are interferon beta (case report) and warfarin (a potential interaction listed in a review). In contrast, a study in which all 52 enrolled patients with lymphoedema (no comparison group is described) were given a combination product of Melilotus, rutin and bromelain for six months reported no side effects and no change in liver function tests; this was a combination product, not sweet clover alone.
